newsitem.title: ITALY: U.N. paints horrific picture of events in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. paints horrific picture of events in Zaire.

text.p: The head of the U.N.'s food aid agency on Wednesday warned of a horrific spectre of events in eastern Zaire, with tens of thousands of people dying or suffering from malnutrition and disease by the end of the month.
"We are seeing the face of hunger in eastern Zaire in a horrible way," said Catherine Bertini, executive director of the World Food Programme (WFP).
"Families are leaving the weak behind as they rush for safety. Bodies dot the roadside and the nearby forests," she told a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome.
Bertini said an international force now in the making must move fast if it is to avert an immense human catastrophe.
"We already know the price of failure," she said in one of the most emotional speeches on the summit's first day.

"Based on our long experience with humanitarian emergencies, we know that within a month, 75,000 more people will succumb to dysentery and cholera...50,000 more children will suffer severe malnutrition, their bellies swollen and distended."
"We must act now in eastern Zaire. And we must act now for all the world's hungry poor," said Bertini, an American.

Canada is offering to lead a multinational military force to bring in the aid to desperate Rwandan and Burundian Hutus in eastern Zaire. U.N. leaders say it could be in place by the weekend following a vote by the Security Council.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Wednesday that President Bill Clinton had decided in principle that the United States would take part in the force.
France, ceding the lead role to Canada because of Rwandan and rebel hostility, said it could have 600 paratroopers in Zaire 24 hours after U.N. approval and 600 more a day later.
Up to 10,000 troops from at least 12 nations including Spain, Italy, South Africa and six other African countries could take part.

WFP spokesman Trevor Rowe said the agency was considering delivering food to refugees in eastern Zaire by air drops. It would be contingent on military teams on the ground to clear the area to prevent accidents.

"We can fly in 100 tonnes of food a day if the area is cleared," Rowe told Reuters at the summit, which is organised by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation. "The down side is that when you do air drops you no longer control distribution. But the situation is so desperate we are considering it."
He said 100 tonnes would provide one week's rations for 50,000 people.

Carol Bellamy, head of the U.N.'s children fund, UNICEF, told the summit that the first victims of the crisis in the Great Lakes region were women and children and that UNICEF was doing all it could to bring them assistance.
